sentences.text: Open almost any kitchen cupboard and you will find a box of baking soda, and almost every home remedy website has a use for it.
Some of those uses are backed by science, some are harmless but pointless, and a few can send people to the emergency room.
In this video, we will separate the useful from the risky, so you know exactly when baking soda helps, how much is too much, and who should leave it in the cupboard.
Disclaimer: This video is for general education only and is not medical advice.
1. Skin Uses
Let us start with the skin, where baking soda is popular for soothing itching and irritation.
A paste made with a little water can calm itching from insect bites and mild stings.
Mix about three parts baking soda with one part water, apply it for a few minutes, and rinse it off.
A lukewarm bath with a quarter to half a cup of baking soda is another common way to ease itching from mild rashes, sunburn, or heat irritation, and some people with eczema find this helpful.
However, your skin has a naturally slightly acidic surface, usually around pH five, which helps protect it from bacteria and keeps it from drying out.
Baking soda is alkaline, so using it too often or too strongly can disrupt this protective layer.
This can lead to dryness, redness, and irritation, especially in people with sensitive skin.
For this reason, do not use baking soda as a daily face scrub, a facial mask, or a deodorant if your skin becomes irritated, because underarm rashes are a common complaint.
Avoid putting it on broken, cut, or severely sunburned skin.
Test a small amount on your forearm first, and stop using it if you notice redness, burning, or itching.
Do not use baking soda to treat acne, blisters, or rashes you do not understand without medical advice, and do not mix it with lemon juice or vinegar on your skin, because that reaction can irritate.
Baking soda should also not be used as a hair wash for long, because it can leave hair dry and brittle.
Moisturise after any baking soda bath to help restore the skin's natural barrier.
Do not use baking soda baths for babies without a doctor's advice, and see a doctor if a rash is spreading, painful, or accompanied by fever.
A soothing paste for a bug bite is fine, but infected skin needs proper treatment.
Another popular use is a foot soak.
A few tablespoons of baking soda in a basin of warm water can soften rough skin and reduce odour, and many people find it relaxing.
Rinse and dry your feet well afterwards, especially between the toes.
If you have diabetes or poor circulation, check with your doctor before soaking your feet, because small problems can become serious.
2. Oral Care
Next, your teeth and mouth.
Baking soda is a gentle abrasive, which means its tiny crystals help scrub away plaque and surface stains without being as harsh as many other abrasives.
Studies have found that toothpastes containing baking soda can remove plaque slightly better than toothpastes without it, and many people like the clean, fresh feeling.
You can brush with a small pinch of baking soda mixed with water, but there is a catch.
Pure baking soda does not contain fluoride, the ingredient that protects enamel against cavities.
For that reason, it is best used occasionally in addition to your normal fluoride toothpaste, not instead of it.
Brush gently, because scrubbing too hard can wear down enamel and irritate your gums.
Baking soda also helps in other ways.

A mouth rinse made with about half a teaspoon of baking soda in a glass of warm water can neutralise acids after a meal or after reflux and may soothe minor mouth irritation, including some canker sores.
Spit it out afterwards, and do not swallow large amounts.
Soaking dentures in a baking soda solution helps remove odours and surface stains, although you should still use your dentist's recommended cleaning method.
A few tips make the experience better.
Wet your toothbrush, dip it lightly in a small amount of baking soda, and brush for no more than a minute with soft strokes, then follow with your normal fluoride toothpaste.
Do this once or twice a week at most.
If your teeth feel sensitive, your gums bleed, or you have braces, implants, or veneers, ask your dentist before using it.
Be careful with whitening claims.
Baking soda may remove some surface stains and make teeth look slightly brighter, but it does not bleach teeth.
If you want whiter teeth, a dentist can recommend safe options.
Baking soda can also help with bad breath by neutralising odour causing acids in the mouth, though it does not fix the cause.
Persistent bad breath may come from gum disease, cavities, a dry mouth, or digestive problems, so see a dentist if it keeps coming back.
Remember that brushing twice a day, cleaning between your teeth, and regular dental check ups are the foundation of oral health.

3. Chemical Facts
Now let us step back and look at what baking soda actually is.
Its chemical name is sodium bicarbonate, and it is a fine white powder that dissolves in water and is mildly alkaline.
When it meets an acid, it reacts and releases carbon dioxide gas, which is why it makes cakes rise and why it fizzes when you add vinegar.
This ability to neutralise acid is the reason behind almost every health use you will hear about.
In daily life, baking soda has many roles beyond health.
Cooks use it to tenderise beans, to brown onions faster, and to balance sour flavours in tomato sauces.
It also absorbs odours in the fridge and helps with cleaning.
Because it is so common, people assume it is safe in any amount, but a product that is safe in a cake is not automatically safe to drink in large doses.
Baking soda is not the same as baking powder.
Baking powder is a mixture that already contains baking soda together with a dry acid and a starch.
If a recipe or a home remedy says baking soda, do not swap in baking powder, and never use it as a replacement for medicine.
Your own body also makes bicarbonate.
It is one of the main buffers that keep your blood within a very narrow pH range, between about 7.35 and 7.45.
Your kidneys and lungs adjust this balance all day long, and this is why claims that baking soda alkalises your body are a myth.
Drinking it does not change the pH of your blood in a healthy person, and a body that is pushed outside that range is a medical emergency, not a health goal.
Now the myths.
Baking soda does not cure cancer, does not detox your liver, does not melt fat, and does not replace a balanced diet or medical treatment.
Videos that promise these results are not based on solid evidence.
The real uses are smaller, more practical, and come with limits.
Buy plain baking soda sold for food use, and keep it in a dry, closed container, away from moisture and strong smells.
Fresh baking soda should fizz when you add a little vinegar, and if it does not, it has lost its strength.
4. Heartburn Relief
The most common health use is quick relief from occasional heartburn and acid indigestion.
Baking soda works as an antacid, which means it neutralises some of the acid in your stomach, and many over the counter antacid products contain sodium bicarbonate.
Relief can begin within minutes, but it is short lived.
If you try it, the usual advice on product labels is to dissolve about half a teaspoon in a full glass of water, drink it slowly, and follow the maximum amount stated on the box.
Do not take it on a very full stomach, because the gas it produces can build up quickly, and there have been rare cases of the stomach being injured.
Do not use it for more than about two weeks without speaking to a doctor.
There are important limits.
Baking soda is high in sodium, and the acid rebound effect, where the stomach makes more acid after the antacid wears off, can make symptoms return.
It is a quick fix for an occasional problem, not a daily habit.
If you have heartburn more than twice a week, trouble swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting, black stools, or chest pain, see a doctor, because these can be signs of a more serious problem.
Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart attack, so seek urgent care when you are not sure.
It also helps to know the other options.
Over the counter antacids that contain calcium carbonate or magnesium, and medicines that reduce acid production, are designed for repeated use and have clearer dosing.

Simple lifestyle steps can also reduce heartburn, such as eating smaller meals, avoiding food within three hours of bedtime, raising the head of your bed, cutting back on spicy and fatty foods, caffeine, and alcohol, and keeping a healthy weight.
Keep a note of how often you need antacids.
If you find yourself reaching for the box regularly, that is a sign to see a doctor, not to take more.
Baking soda should also not be given to young children, and it is wise to check with a doctor if you are pregnant, since the sodium load and the gas can cause problems.
Sip it slowly, because gulping it down quickly increases gas and bloating, and make sure it is fully dissolved before you drink.
5. Safety Limits
Finally, the most important section, which is about how much is too much.
Baking soda is high in sodium.

Half a teaspoon contains roughly 600 milligrams of sodium, and a full teaspoon contains well over a thousand, while health guidelines suggest that most adults should stay under about 2,300 milligrams of sodium a day from all sources.
Taking baking soda for heartburn adds a lot to that total.
Too much baking soda can cause serious problems.
These include vomiting, diarrhea, extreme thirst, muscle weakness or twitching, confusion, and a condition called metabolic alkalosis, in which the blood becomes too alkaline.
It can also lower potassium levels, cause fluid retention, and raise blood pressure.
If someone swallows a large amount, or develops severe vomiting, confusion, muscle spasms, or a very slow or irregular heartbeat, they need urgent medical care.
Some people should avoid taking baking soda by mouth unless a doctor says it is fine.
This includes people with high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease, liver disease, or swelling in the legs, anyone on a low sodium diet, pregnant women, and young children.
Baking soda can also affect how some medicines are absorbed, so take it at least two hours apart from other medicines, and ask your pharmacist.
Some athletes use sodium bicarbonate supplements for short, intense exercise, but the amounts used cause stomach upset in many people, so it should only be tried with professional guidance.
Keep the box away from children and pets, and label it clearly so it is not confused with sugar, flour, or salt.
If a child or pet swallows a large amount, call a poison control centre or a doctor right away.
Do not try to make them vomit unless a professional tells you to.
Remember that cheap and common does not always mean harmless.
The golden rule is simple: use the smallest amount that works, for the shortest time, and stop if you feel unwell.
If you take any regular medicine, check with your pharmacist first, because the sodium and the change in stomach acid can affect how some medicines work.
To wrap up, baking soda is a cheap, useful product for occasional heartburn, a gentle brush for your teeth, and a soothing paste for itchy skin, but it is not a cure for everything.
Use small amounts, follow the label, and speak to a doctor if you have a medical condition or take regular medicine.
If this video helped you, share it with someone who loves home remedies, and leave a comment telling us how you use baking soda.
Thank you for watching, and we will see you in the next video.
